name: The Task Creator
oneLiner: Batch-creates ADO Task work items from an in-file plan — each fully populated and parented under its user story via a Hierarchy link.
lead: When a batch of work is planned — each item with title, description, owner, and acceptance criteria — someone still has to key it into ADO. This agent does that data entry: it POSTs each Task fully populated and parents it under the correct user story via a `Hierarchy-Reverse` link, so nothing is orphaned.
chore: Creating a dozen tasks by hand is repetitive and error-prone. Per task: open a blank form, paste title, description, and acceptance criteria, set priority, add tags, then link the parent — sometimes two parents. Twelve times over, it's easy to drop a link, mistype a tag, or skip the acceptance criteria entirely.
instead: The agent holds the plan and creates each Task in one run — title, description, acceptance criteria, priority, and tags all set. It links each to its first parent during creation, and PATCHes extra `Hierarchy-Reverse` links for any task with multiple parents. It closes with a summary table of what got created and where it landed.
whyItMatters: Consistent, fully-linked tasks mean the agreed plan lands in ADO exactly as intended, with nothing dropped.

howItWorks.step: For each task it builds the full field set — title, description, acceptance criteria, priority, tags — and POSTs it as a Task in one request, with the first parent's `Hierarchy-Reverse` link attached inline.
howItWorks.explain:
A Task is created with a **JSON-Patch document** — an array of `add` ops keyed by ADO **reference name** (`System.Title`, `Microsoft.VSTS.Common.AcceptanceCriteria`, etc.), not UI labels. Two ADO quirks are handled inline: description and acceptance-criteria fields render **HTML**, so literal newlines are converted to `
` or they'd collapse to one line; and priority is stored numerically, so `priorityMap` translates a `High`/`Medium` label to ADO's 1–4, defaulting to `2` for anything unmapped. The first parent is linked **during creation** by appending a `Hierarchy-Reverse` relation (from the child's side, *Reverse* points up to the parent — Forward would nest the story under the task instead), so the Task is never momentarily orphaned. Note the endpoint `wit/workitems/$Task` — the literal `$` prefix on the type name is required by the create API — and the content type must be `application/json-patch+json`, not plain JSON.

howItWorks.step: When a task has multiple parents, it PATCHes each extra `Hierarchy-Reverse` link with its own follow-up request.
howItWorks.explain: A work item's create call attaches only the *first* parent link, so additional parents are added afterward one at a time. This is why it's a **PATCH** to `wit/workitems/{taskId}` (updating an existing item) rather than the `POST .../$Task` create — but the body is the same single `add` op on `/relations/-`, appending another `Hierarchy-Reverse` relation to the parent. It returns the bare `response.ok` boolean rather than throwing, so the caller can record one bad parent link as a per-task failure and keep going instead of aborting the whole batch. Same `application/json-patch+json` content type the create call needs.

howItWorks.step: It prints a summary table — task, new work item ID, parent(s), and Created/Failed — plus each item's URL.
howItWorks.explain: The driver loop encodes the two-phase linking: `createTask` attaches parent `[0]` inline, so the follow-up loop starts at **index 1** to PATCH only the *extra* parents, and `linked` seeds with `parentUS[0]` because that first link already succeeded as part of creation. Link tracking is granular — a parent ID is pushed into `linked` only when `linkToParent` returns `ok`, so a task can end up created-but-partially-linked, and that shows up honestly in the summary rather than being reported as fully done. A failed `createTask` records a null-ID row instead of crashing the batch, so one bad task never stops the rest. The final pass prints a Markdown table where `status` is derived purely from whether an `adoId` exists (`Created` vs `Failed`) and `N/A`/`-` stand in for the missing ID and empty parent list.

examples.caption: Create a planned batch of tasks
examples.input: An in-file plan of 6 tasks, each with description, acceptance criteria, owner, and parent story.
examples.output: Created all 6 Tasks (#701–#706), each `Hierarchy-Reverse`-linked to its parent story. Printed a summary table with each URL.

examples.caption: A task with two parents
examples.input: A task parented under both story #204 and story #207.
examples.output: Created the task with the #204 link inline, then PATCHed the second link to #207. Both `Hierarchy-Reverse` links confirmed.

examples.caption: One link PATCH fails
examples.input: Create the batch; one parent ID is invalid.
examples.output: 5 of 6 tasks fully linked. One task created but its link PATCH to the bad parent returned non-OK — flagged in the summary for manual fix.

underHood.heading: Populating the Task fields
underHood.input: A task's title, description, acceptance criteria, priority, and tags.
underHood.output: A single POST that creates the Task, fully populated.

underHood.heading: Linking the first parent
underHood.whenRuns: Inline in the same POST that creates the task.
underHood.input: The task's primary parent story ID.
underHood.output: The new Task appears nested under that story in ADO.

underHood.heading: PATCHing extra parents
underHood.whenRuns: Right after creation, only for tasks with more than one parent.
underHood.input: The new task's ID and each additional parent ID.
underHood.output: One more `Hierarchy-Reverse` link per extra parent, each confirmed independently.

underHood.heading: Printing the summary
underHood.whenRuns: After every task in the batch has been attempted.
underHood.input: Each task's outcome — created or failed — and its links.
underHood.output: A markdown summary table (task, new work item ID, parent, status) plus each item's URL.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Azure DevOps access and a **PAT** scoped to create work items.
The planned batch written out — title, description, acceptance criteria, priority, tags, and parent story ID(s) per item.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the engine that runs the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is TypeScript run under Node — a one-time per-machine install.

steps.label: Clone the agent and install its dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the one dependency this script needs to talk to the ADO REST API.
steps.firstRun: Cold install — a minute or two.

steps.label: Set the write PAT (env var).
steps.why: The one secret the script needs. Unlike the other agents, this one hard-codes its target org/project and the task plan in the source file rather than taking flags — see the next step.

steps.label: Edit the source and fill in your batch.
steps.why: This script targets one specific batch, not a generic importer — the org/project and the `tasks` array are constants in the file. Editing them here is this agent's 'input' step.

steps.label: Run it and read the printed summary table.
steps.why: Creates every task in your `tasks` array, links each to its parent(s), and prints a table of what was created and where it landed — plus each new item's URL.
steps.firstRun: Creates the whole batch from scratch.
steps.rerun: Non-idempotent — re-running creates a duplicate batch. Re-run only after clearing or editing the `tasks` array.

inputs.name: the `tasks` array (in-file)
inputs.desc: Each planned item's title, description, acceptance criteria, priority, tags, and one or more parent story IDs.

inputs.name: ADO_ORGANIZATION / ADO_PROJECT (in-file constants)
inputs.desc: Which ADO org/project to create the tasks in.

inputs.name: ADO_PAT_WRITE (environment variable)
inputs.desc: The PAT authorizing the script to create work items.

outputs.name: new Tasks in ADO
outputs.desc: Each fully populated and nested under its parent story (or stories) via `Hierarchy-Reverse`.

outputs.name: console summary table
outputs.desc: Task, new work item ID, parent, and status (Created/Failed) for every item, plus each URL.

runbook.rerun: Non-idempotent — each run creates brand-new tasks with no memory of prior runs, so re-running the same `tasks` array duplicates the whole batch. Clear the array (or comment out already-created items) before re-running.
runbook.integrate: Treat this as a one-off migration script per planning batch, not a scheduled service — copy it, swap in the next batch's `tasks`, run once, then set it aside until the next planning round.

video.caption: A 2-3 minute screen recording: fill in a planned batch and create it in ADO.
script: Open the script file and the terminal side by side.
Say: 'This one is simpler — the plan lives right in the file. Let's fill it in and run it.'
Run `node -v` and `npm install` (or note it's already done).
Scroll to the `tasks` array; point out one item's title, description, done-checklist, and parent story ID.
Set `export ADO_PAT_WRITE=...`; say this is the only secret it needs.
Run `npm run ado:tasks`; narrate the created lines as each task appears.
Point out the second-parent case — one task linking to two stories — and its two confirmation lines.
Read the printed summary table out loud — task, new ID, parent, status.
Open one of the printed links in the browser to show the task nested under its story.
Close: 'One run, whole plan on the board, nothing typed by hand.'
